=Write a cold email opening for a technical recruitment agency, triggered by a recent funding round.

Variables:

Recipient full name: {{ $('Webhook2').item.json.body.result.personFullName }}
Recipient role: {{ $('Webhook2').item.json.body.result.personJobTitle }}
Funding info: {{ $json.jobOpeningTitle }}
Company: {{ $json.companyName }}
Location: {{ $json.location }}

Context:
The "Funding info" field contains a funding round type and amount in the format "round_type - $XM" (e.g. "series a - $15.0M", "seed - $3.2M", "pre-seed - $0.8M"). Extract only the round type. Never use the dollar amount anywhere in the output.

Goal:
Create a short, natural-sounding cold email opening. The tone is casual and slightly imperfect on purpose, like a quick human note. The agency recruits engineers for startups and tech companies. Their edge is that they are engineers and former engineering managers who now do recruitment, so they understand what a good engineer actually looks like.

VARIANT OUTPUT:
You must output ALL THREE variants for every input. Each variant uses a different angle but the same personalization (first name, company, round type).

--- VARIANT A: Pain + Profiles ---
Line 1: Noticed [Company] closed a [Round Type] recently.
Line 2: After a raise, engineering hiring usually becomes the bottleneck and most generalist recruiters make it worse.
Line 3: We are engineers who moved into recruitment, ran eng teams ourselves, so we actually know what good looks like technically. We have a few vetted profiles that could be a fit.
Line 4: Would it be useful if I sent over a few anonymous profles?

--- VARIANT B: Pattern Recognition ---
Line 1: Noticed [Company] closed a [Round Type] recently.
Line 2: Engineering hiring usually becomes the bottleneck right after a raise. Small team, fast roadmap, no time to sort through 200 applicants.
Line 3: I am an engineer myself, so I know what to filter for before anyone wastes your time.
Line 4: Worth a 15-minute call to see if it fits?

--- VARIANT C: Candidate-Led ---
Line 1: Noticed [Company] closed a [Round Type] recently.
Line 2: We are currently working with a couple of senior engineers who are open to new roles. Strong profiles, all technically vetted by our team since we are engineers ourselves.
Line 3: Would any of that be relevant to what you are building?

Output format:
Return valid JSON only, no preamble, no markdown. Output an object with all three variants:
{"round_type":"", "variant_a":"", "variant_b":"", "variant_c":""}

round_type: the funding round type extracted from the funding info field, lowercase (e.g. "seed", "series a", "pre-seed").
variant_a: the full Variant A email opening as plain text, with each block separated by \n\n.
variant_b: the full Variant B email opening as plain text, with each block separated by \n\n.
variant_c: the full Variant C email opening as plain text, with each block separated by \n\n.
If personFullName, funding info, or companyName is missing or empty, return only:
{"error":"missing_required_field"}
location is optional.

Rules:

Start with: Hi [First Name], Use only the recipient's first name, extracted from the full name.
COMPANY NAME formatting:
a. Strip ONLY these exact legal suffixes if present: GmbH, Ltd, Inc., AG, UG, LLC, SE, BV, SAS, NV
b. Do NOT strip words like: Network, Group, Solutions, Technologies, Systems, Services
c. Do not abbreviate or expand the company name.
d. Casing:
If the remaining name already contains an internal capital letter, keep it exactly as-is. Examples: DataCamp, GitHub, iText
If the remaining name is all-caps and 2 to 5 letters long, keep it exactly as-is because it is likely an acronym. Examples: EIDU, SAP, BMW, AWS
If the remaining name is all-caps and one word, keep it exactly as-is because it is likely a brand name. Examples: AIWORKS, DEEPTECH, CODEVERSE
Otherwise, if the remaining name is all-caps or all-lowercase, capitalize the first letter of each word and lowercase the rest. Examples: datalytics -> Datalytics ; ACME SOLUTIONS -> Acme Solutions
ROUND TYPE formatting for use in line 1:
Capitalize naturally: "seed" -> "Seed", "series a" -> "Series A", "pre-seed" -> "Pre-Seed"
Never include the dollar amount anywhere in the email. Mentioning the exact number feels automated and database-scraped.
Use the exact lines specified in each variant. Do not mix lines across variants. Do not rephrase or add words.
Each variant's lines must be separated by a blank line (use \n\n between blocks).

Hard constraints:
6. Never include em dashes.
7. No exclamation marks.
8. Do not use the word "just".
9. Do not add a sender name or signature.
10. Do NOT congratulate them on the raise. No "Congrats", "Exciting", "Impressive", or "Great news".
11. Do NOT mention the dollar amount. Ever. Under any circumstances.
12. Keep the tone direct, casual, and human. Not salesy.
13. The company name appears exactly once per variant, in line 1.
14. The round type appears exactly once per variant, in line 1.
15. The only personalization is the first name, company name, and round type.
16. Do not add anything before or after the JSON.
17. Do not pitch, over-explain, or add agency history beyond what is written in the variant.
18. Total email body per variant must be under 100 words.
19. Deliberate typos in the variants (profles) must be kept exactly as written.

Example output:
{"round_type":"series a", "variant_a":"Hi Victor,\n\nNoticed LemonEdge closed a Series A recently.\n\nAfter a raise, engineering hiring usually becomes the bottleneck and most generalist recruiters make it worse.\n\nWe are engineers who moved into recruitment, ran eng teams ourselves, so we actually know what good looks like technically. We have a few vetted profiles that could be a fit.\n\nWould it be useful if I sent over a few anonymous profles?", "variant_b":"Hi Victor,\n\nNoticed LemonEdge closed a Series A recently.\n\nEngineering hiring usually becomes the bottleneck right after a raise. Small team, fast roadmap, no time to sort through 200 applicants.\n\nI am an engineer myself, so I know what to filter for before anyone wastes your time.\n\nWorth a 15-minute call to see if it fits?", "variant_c":"Hi Victor,\n\nNoticed LemonEdge closed a Series A recently.\n\nWe are currently working with a couple of senior engineers who are open to new roles. Strong profiles, all technically vetted by our team since we are engineers ourselves.\n\nWould any of that be relevant to what you are building?"}

=Write a cold email opening for a technical recruitment agency, triggered by a job change signal.

Company: {{ $json.companyName }}

Goal:
Create a short, natural-sounding cold email opening. The tone is casual and slightly imperfect on purpose, like a quick human note. The agency recruits engineers for startups and tech companies. Their edge is that they are engineers and former engineering managers who now do recruitment, so they understand what a good engineer actually looks like.

Line 1: Noticed you recently joined [Company] as [Role].

Line 3: We are engineers who moved into recruitment, ran eng teams ourselves, so we actually know what the bar should look like. We have a few vetted profiles that might be relevant.
Line 4: Would it be useful if I sent over a few anonymous profles?

Line 1: Noticed you recently joined [Company] as [Role].
Line 2: The first 90 days in a new eng leadership role is usually when hiring decisions get made, before the roadmap locks in.
Line 3: We are engineers ourselves, so we handle the technical screening before anything reaches you.
Line 4: Worth a quick call to see if the timing fits?

Line 1: Noticed you recently joined [Company] as [Role].
Line 2: We work specifically with engineering leaders, not HR. Our team are engineers ourselves so we know what the role actually demands technically.
